chief_complaint: vaginal soreness and memory loss after a party
hpi_details: 23F presenting to the ED reporting she woke up at an acquaintance's flat 10 hours ago after drinking at a party, with no memory of the preceding events. She complains of vaginal soreness and notes her underwear is torn. She has not showered or changed clothes since waking up. She is not on any regular contraception, and her LMP was 2 weeks ago. She is seeking evaluation for potential pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, and expresses uncertainty about reporting the incident to the police.
ideas: patient suspects she may have been drugged and sexually assaulted while unconscious
concerns: patient is terrified of becoming pregnant or catching an STI, and feels overwhelmed by the idea of a police investigation
expectations: wants emergency contraception, testing for infections, and guidance on her options without being pressured to involve law enforcement
pmh: No significant past medical or psychiatric history. Regular menstrual cycles.
social_hx: University student. Drinks alcohol occasionally; denies illicit drug use. Non-smoker.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Mandatory reporting laws vary by jurisdiction, but generally, competent adults have the autonomy to decide whether to report sexual assault to law enforcement.
While forensic evidence collection is ideal within 72 hours, some evidence can occasionally be collected up to 120 hours post-assault, depending on local protocols.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the provider must report the assault to the police even if the adult patient declines.
Performing a routine pelvic exam immediately in the ED before discussing or coordinating a forensic examination (rape kit), which could destroy evidence.
Failing to consider drug-facilitated sexual assault (DFSA) and omitting time-sensitive urine toxicology screening.
Using judgmental language or questioning the patient's choices regarding alcohol consumption or attending the party.
core_concepts: Providing a trauma-informed, non-judgmental environment is paramount to ensure patient safety and empower their decision-making.

Forensic evidence collection is time-sensitive (typically within 72-120 hours) and must be offered before the patient showers or changes clothes, ideally via specialized centers (e.g., Sunflower Center in South Korea).
Medical management must prioritize the prevention of unintended pregnancy (emergency contraception) and sexually transmitted infections (empirical STI treatment, HIV PEP, Hepatitis B vaccination).
Reporting to law enforcement for adult survivors of sexual assault is strictly the patient's choice and should never be a prerequisite for receiving medical care.
dangerous_errors: Pressuring or forcing the patient to report the incident to law enforcement against her will.
Allowing or suggesting the patient shower, use the restroom, or change clothes before a forensic exam is offered or completed.
Missing the window for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which should be initiated within 72 hours of the exposure.
Neglecting to offer emergency contraception to a patient of reproductive age not on birth control.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: vaginal soreness and memory loss after a party

Key HPI features: Waking up in a different location 10 hours ago with amnesia of the night, physical signs of potential trauma (torn underwear, vaginal soreness), and an unwashed state preserving potential evidence.

Objective/Exam findings: Patient appears distressed and anxious. Vital signs are stable. Patient is wearing the same clothes from the night before. Genitourinary exam deferred pending patient consent and forensic examiner availability to avoid destroying evidence.
Relevant background/PMH: LMP 2 weeks ago (potentially periovulatory), no current contraception.
management_principles: Ensure patient safety and obtain explicit consent at every step of the evaluation.
Coordinate prompt forensic evidence collection (e.g., referral to a Sunflower Center) as the patient is within the optimal time window and has not washed.
Collect baseline urine toxicology to evaluate for drug-facilitated sexual assault, along with baseline STI/HIV testing and a pregnancy test.
Offer and administer emergency contraception, empiric STI prophylaxis (e.g., Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, Metronidazole), HIV PEP evaluation, and Hepatitis B vaccination/immunoglobulin if indicated.
Provide immediate psychological support and connect the patient with specialized sexual assault advocacy resources.

reference_soap.objective: Vitals: T 36.8 C, HR 88, BP 115/75 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air. General: Alert, oriented, but appears anxious, tearful, and distressed. Wearing clothes from the previous night. Genitourinary exam: Deferred in the ED to preserve forensic evidence, pending evaluation by a specialized forensic examiner (Sunflower Center).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Ensure patient safety and employ a trauma-informed approach. 2. Counsel on the time-sensitive nature of forensic evidence collection; facilitate immediate referral/transfer to the Sunflower Center for a forensic exam, advising her not to shower, wash, or change clothes. 3. Obtain baseline labs: urine toxicology (to evaluate for drug-facilitated assault), urine pregnancy test, baseline HIV and syphilis serology. 4. Administer emergency contraception (e.g., Levonorgestrel or Ulipristal acetate) and empiric STI prophylaxis (Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, Metronidazole) plus HIV PEP if indicated per risk assessment. 5. Provide psychological support and inform her that reporting to the police is entirely her decision.

learning_objectives: Demonstrate a trauma-informed, empathetic, and non-judgmental communication style when interviewing a survivor of sexual assault.
Prioritize the preservation of forensic evidence by advising the patient not to wash or change clothes and facilitating appropriate specialized referral.
Identify the core medical interventions required for acute sexual assault, including emergency contraception, STI/HIV prophylaxis, and toxicology screening.
Respect and support patient autonomy regarding the decision to report the assault to law enforcement.

teaching.diagnosis: Acute sexual assault (possible drug-facilitated sexual assault)

must_ask.objective: Establish a safe and supportive environment
must_ask.say: I am so sorry this happened to you. You are in a safe place now, and we are here to help you.

must_ask.objective: Assess the timeline to determine forensic window
must_ask.say: Can you tell me roughly how many hours it has been since you woke up?

must_ask.objective: Check if evidence has been preserved
must_ask.say: Have you showered, bathed, or changed your clothes since this happened?
Do you remember what you were drinking, or if anyone could have put something in your drink?

must_ask.objective: Determine pregnancy risk based on menstrual cycle
must_ask.say: When was the first day of your last menstrual period?

must_ask.objective: Address patient's concerns regarding police involvement
must_ask.say: I understand you are unsure about the police. Please know that reporting is entirely your choice, and you will receive medical care regardless of what you decide.

must_ask.objective: Explain the role of specialized forensic centers
must_ask.say: There is a specialized center called the Sunflower Center where they can collect evidence gently, just in case you decide to report it later. Would you like to hear more about that?

teaching.one_liner: 23-year-old female presenting with amnesia, vaginal soreness, and torn clothing after a party, requiring time-sensitive medical prophylaxis and forensic evaluation.
red_flags: Unexplained genital soreness and torn clothing
Waking up in an unfamiliar or unexpected location
Delayed presentation due to fear or confusion

history.answer: I woke up this morning at an acquaintance's flat with my underwear torn and pain down below, and I have no memory of what happened last night.
Thank you, I feel much safer talking here privately, and I am grateful for your reassurance about confidentiality.
I woke up around 8 a.m. today, roughly ten hours ago, at an acquaintance's apartment after attending a party there last night.
I only know the host casually through university classmates, but I honestly don't know who stayed in the room or who might have assaulted me.
I do not remember the act itself, but I woke up with severe vaginal soreness and my underwear was torn.
I was so scared and confused that I haven't showered, bathed, or changed out of the clothes I wore last night.
I only had two drinks early in the evening, but then I experienced a sudden and complete blackout, which has never happened to me before.
My vaginal area feels raw and sore, but I do not have bleeding cuts, broken bones, or severe pain anywhere else.
No, I don't recall anyone choking my neck, and I don't feel any lumps or tenderness on my head.
I felt groggy and slightly nauseous when I first woke up, but I don't have persistent dizziness, vomiting, or difficulty swallowing.
No, nothing like this has ever happened to me before.
I left that apartment right away; I have my own studio apartment where I live alone, so I do not have to see that person.
No, I live by myself near campus and do not have any children or family members depending on me.
No, I am not in a relationship, and nobody has been stalking, monitoring, or controlling me.
I feel terrified, completely on edge, and my hands won't stop shaking.
No, I have no desire to end my life or hurt myself; I just want to get through this and make sure I am healthy.
I haven't told my family or friends yet because I feel overwhelmed and ashamed, and I've never contacted crisis counseling before.
I urgently want emergency contraception and tests for infections, but I feel terrified of a police investigation and don't know if I can handle reporting it yet.
If a specialized center can preserve the evidence safely while allowing me to decide on reporting later, I would like to do that.
My last menstrual period started exactly two weeks ago, and my cycles are usually very regular every twenty-eight days.
I am not using any birth control, and since this happened right in the middle of my cycle, I am terrified of becoming pregnant.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have never been diagnosed with any illnesses.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, non-prescription drugs, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medicines.
No, I have never smoked.
I drink socially on occasion with friends, usually just a beer or two, and I have never lost my memory like this from alcohol alone.
No, I have never used any recreational drugs or illegal substances.
I am a third-year university student living alone in an off-campus studio apartment.
Both of my parents are healthy with no major genetic or medical illnesses.

Alert and oriented, but visibly anxious, tearful, and wearing unwashed clothing from the previous night.
Oriented to person, place, and time, with clear speech, intact comprehension, and situational distress.
No visible petechiae, abrasions, lacerations, or contusions on exposed areas of the face, neck, arms, or legs.
Chest wall is symmetric with no ecchymoses, deformities, or palpation tenderness.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended without abrasions, scars, or contusions.
Soft and non-tender across all four quadrants without guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable masses.
Torn underwear is noted; external inspection is otherwise deferred pending specialized forensic examination to avoid contaminating evidence.
Deferred in the emergency department to preserve forensic evidence pending transfer to a specialized forensic support center.
